utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I just inquire whether the protective measures for Witness Q, especially also if voice distortion is effective or can be made effective. I get a confirmation from the Registry that it is. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If the Bench authorises me to do so in this respect, before the witness here, the Defence would like to make a brief preliminary statement. Thank you, sir. Chairman -- President, Judges, I would just like to express the position of the Defence counsel in relation to what happened yesterday. We are awaiting -- I am referring to what happened yesterday. As I was saying, we are awaiting an addition to your decision, I suppose, but the Defence counsel as a whole would like to proceed and make a brief statement. According to the historic words, whoever comes too late will be punished for life, and I believe it is the duty of the Defence counsel of his Excellency General Galic, but also the other assistance of justice such as lawyers to raise this point at this stage. We looked at the photo yesterday and we saw a problem in relation to what we normally call manipulation of documents. The Defence knows full well that we have no way of requesting an original to be produced and either from the Prosecution or any other authority in possession of the original document. What the Defence would like to stress is that with respect to this kaleidoscope of truth, and everybody sees what they wish to see, but there are quite a few things that can be found there. Yesterday, we saw here a reference to a mass grave and it was a public -- it was public knowledge, and several hundred, and perhaps several thousand, bodies were thrown into that mass grave. Now, the Defence is certain that such a discovery would not have been something to which international justice would have remained indifferent and it is up to us, Judge, to decide in what way we shall have to act in relation to that piece of documentation. And the Defence believes that it is within the power of the international institutions, if they feel it is necessary, to come out with an injunction and require -- request the original of that document to be produced. That is what I wanted to say, and thank you very much indeed for having listened to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I will not make on behalf of this Chamber any observation at this very moment. I will discuss the matter with other members of the Chamber and, if appropriate, I will address the matter soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any observation from the Prosecution in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am grateful, Mr. President, with your leave. Firstly, may I say that unhappily many crimes were committed in the theatre of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these crimes, insofar as we are aware of them, are being investigated, have to some extent been investigated, and prosecutions for a variety of crimes where there is sufficient evidence have been made. Insofar as this case is concerned, we would invite the Defence and the Court to -- well, the Defence in particular -- to review, I think it is paragraph 216 of the Prosecution's brief, which clearly and succinctly states the position of international humanitarian law, in respect to reciprocity. I think it is called the tu quoque principle. The fact that other crimes have been committed in this theatre or in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not of direct relevance to this case, but it is to this Tribunal and we do everything in our power to investigate them and to see that justice is done. May it please you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. It was just one of the issues I would like to discuss with my colleagues, the relevance of the part of the document mentioned by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Then, Mr. Stamp, I think we are at a point where the Prosecution could re-examine Witness Q since all protective measures are in effect. Please, Mr. Usher, could you escort Mr. Q into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, may I remind you that, perhaps unnecessarily, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness Q, yesterday the Defence referred to the incident of the 22nd of September -- I beg your pardon, the 22nd of January, 1994, and then read from your statement, and perhaps I will just reread it from the transcript: "The BSA fires shells from close to our position to confuse investigators." Now, you said that you would have said that in your statement. Can you recall if you said that in respect to the incident of the 22nd of January or in respect of the incident of the 9th of November, 1993? If you cannot recall, you may review your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I have said it in relation to any of the two incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you understand English a little? Can you read your statement in English?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure I can understand the entire statement in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: With your leave, Mr. President, I am just going to ask him to have a look at a document and answer a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What document do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is a statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me, could the counsel's microphone be somehow adjusted? Because of the voice distortion, we can barely hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are first trying to solve the microphone problem with Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp, if you may have noticed, the interpreters have difficulties in hearing you, so perhaps you speak close to the microphone. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see in what language my learned friend intends to submit this, in English or in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you intend to present to the witness, in which language? Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether you are listening to the French or not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was listening to the English channel for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French booth would like for the microphone of Mr. Stamp to be raised closer to him so that he can speak close into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the same applies to Mr. Piletta-Zanin's microphone, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe this should be sufficient. Could the witness be shown this statement in B/C/S, in the language of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just refresh your memory for us and tell us firstly if you made that statement, and if you did, in relation to which incident you made the statement; was it the 9th of November incident or the 22nd of January incident?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the case of the 9th, 1993 at Zavnobih Square and the square of Rade Koncara.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can't hear my friend's interpretation. I don't know whether I am being punished on purpose or is it just a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment, please, because the French booth is resuming the answer of the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions of this witness. Could the document be returned to me? That, Mr. President, Your Honours, may it please you, is the re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge El Mahdi has one or more questions to you, Mr. Q. Questioned by the Court: JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It seems to me, Witness, that you have had the possibility to access the register which refers to the incidents regarding some shelling. Do you remember approximately how many such incidents there were every month? Do you have any statistical information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, myself, did not keep track in that way. I don't have any statistical information. I had the notes pertaining to my own investigation. Unfortunately, I don't have them on me today. But this register did exist, and what was entered there were any operations carried out by people on duty, by officers on duty. Once they came back to the office, it was their duty to enter the data pertaining to that investigation into the register since we tend to carry out all sorts of investigations involving crime. Every time there was an investigation, there was a reference to the number, the description of the case, and all the other relevant data. For each individual year, we've got one, two, three, or more registers, depending on how many cases of crime we've had. In case one single book suffices, okay. That ends with the date of the 25th of December of any given year and then it is stored in the archives. Since all of that is at the office, it is a part of our official record and it is in the archive, and it is only if you get in touch with the people in charge that you can gain access to such archives. That is the still the current practice. That's the same sort of practice that we had before. It was standard practice and it still exists. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, but you, yourself, for example, do you remember how many such incidents have you, yourself, investigated? For example, how many a month, how many in a day, how many in a quarter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: With reference to that specific period, I can't remember exactly how many cases a day. Sometimes there were more; sometimes less and perhaps even none in a single day. But I can't tell you the exact figure because I am in the same job today. So the percentage tended to go up but I can't remember the exact number of cases I had to deal with in that particular period. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes, I am not referring to investigations as such in general. What I am referring to are shellings. Did you have several teams? How many teams did you have? If possible, if you can remember, I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say, well, from the beginning of my career there, until the end of the hostilities, I myself carried out 52 on-site investigations with reference to various shelling or people being injured and wounded by snipers, so things having to do with the warfare. And that is what I said in my statement, 52 investigations pertaining to the hostilities. But I can't really remember each individual case. All that is entered into the registers I was referring to earlier on. On a daily basis, we had to enter all this into the register. And I don't suppose there will be any problem in checking it out, obviously. Apart from myself and my own investigations, there were other cases elsewhere in town and my colleagues went out carry out on-site investigations. They were trained in much the same way as I was, and on the days I was off duty or if I was somewhere else or people from other police stations did the same, so all that was entered into the same register. The whole range of activities of our police department would be entered into the register for any given year. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Q, I have some additional questions to you as well, but could perhaps first be placed in front of the witness Exhibit P3681. Not on the ELMO, but just in front of him, just the top page. Mr. Q, you have answered some questions yesterday about the bottom of this document. You read a few parts of it. So it's the lower part of the document I am asking you about. Did you make this entry in this register?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. And my name is not mentioned in this part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you involved in whatever way in making this entry in the register? So even if you would not have written it yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't. It has nothing to do with my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that you are not involved in the investigation which appears in this part of the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in that investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any information about that investigation or the results of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just the words that I have read out to you. That was the information I had. It was open to all members of staff. It is a register where we make our own entries and, of course, when we do so we get the opportunity to read other entries. As to everything else, I had no direct contact with any of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do the names of colleagues of yours appear in that entry who were involved in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this register is a document where you enter the date, what happened, the site, the description, and who was involved in the on site investigation. So the column, the one before last, in the lower part of this section, you can see the name of the person in charge, and in case it was a bigger team, you get all the names. In case there was an investigating magistrate present, you get his name and the prosecutor's name and the experts' name, the police officers' names. They should all be entered in this column, the one before last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one other question. Could please this document be removed and returned to the Registry. We have seen a photograph with a yellow line on it and you explained to us that this was something to -- that was used to measure. Would you measure from the photographs or would you measure on the spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the measurements themselves, I could measure the distance from one trace to the other. The measurements that should have been used in order to calculate and in order to come up with ballistic proof, well, the ballistic experts would have had to do that: What sort of projectile it was, what sort of angle it landed at, it was their job. All I had to do was take pictures. And the picture where you did see that yellow tape was meant to be used in order for us to be able to tell the distance. Because when the picture itself was taken, of course if you come close to what you taking a photograph of, the appearance of your subject is quite different from what it would be if you stepped further back. So this yellow tape, I don't know what photo exactly it was on. It was meant to give us the sense of proportion when looking at the pictures, people who were not on the site, in fact, so as not to get the wrong ideas to the size of this hole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Q. That was a mistake, that Judge Nieto-Navia still had a question for you but I knew it not yet at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Q, I would like to make a question on this document, 3681. I think that you don't have to look at it again, but I would like -- I don't remember if you said so, but I would like to know, where is this, the original? Where is the original of this document filed? Who has this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q [Resumed]
utterances.text: That document is the book of records which is at the archive of the Ministry of the Interior of Canton of Sarajevo. That used to be the centre of the public security services. Now it is the Ministry of the Interior of the Canton of Sarajevo. And all registers, all books of records starting from 1993, 1994 onwards, are stored in that archive. I really don't see there would be any impediment or any problem for you to get to see them. I don't know what the procedure is. You would be more familiar with the procedure than I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry, but it is my task to see that justice is done. I believe that I saw on the screen briefly the document concerned. This witness is a protected witness and he told us that his name was on that document -- was in that document. This document was shown inadvertently on the screen and, therefore, I believe that the Chamber should take the necessary measures so that the witness remains protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, may I ask you -- I don't know whether -- was it from a distance or not? If it is from a great distance, it would not be legible, but I didn't notice it because I was looking at the transcript. But if we wait until the first break, we might be too late. So, therefore, Madam Registrar, could you please give instructions that the videotape in that respect is reviewed on whether there is any -- if it is really from a great distance, it makes no difference, I think. But we will check that and have it redacted, if necessary. Meanwhile, Mr. Q, I -- Madam Registrar is taking the necessary steps in order to make your protection as effective as possible. This concludes your examination as a witness in this courtroom. You have answered the questions not only from the parties, but also questions from the Judges and you will be aware that this Chamber hears the testimony given by those who were present at the relevant times at the relevant places and hear what answers the witnesses give on the questions of the parties and the Judges. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague and we wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just informed that the picture, the video picture was such that it would not jeopardise the protection of the witness so a redaction is not needed. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document Exhibit P3681, logbook entries and photographs, Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you wanted to object --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. My objection has to do, as I have already said, that this document did not seem to us to be a document which was completely authentic and it would seem to us -- it seems that it was manipulated, and I was speaking about the first page of this set of documents. And on the other hand, I made a general remark that there was -- we did not have enough time to prepare for these two photographs. The photograph, my objection also concerns the second photograph. Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether the original was manipulated or not or corrected or not, that is not an issue of admissibility of this document. And the Chamber further notes that the testimony of the witness was not related to the part of which the Defence has argued, that there was a manipulation of this document, but rather of the previous entry. The witness has testified that he doesn't know anything on the last line of the document. And of course the Defence, if it turns out to be a relevant issue for this case, of course is entirely free to call witnesses to testify on other entries. The Chamber has indicated that if the Defence would not have had enough time to prepare for the cross-examination, that they could indicate so in order to recall the witness. Until now, I am saying this quite clearly. Until now, we have noticed that the problems of the Defence in respect of this document seem to go rather to the last line than to the previous line on which the -- about which the witness testified in relation to the investigations he was participating in. The document is -- documents, that means the register and the photos and also the black and white photos with the subscripts, are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps our first P3681 should be admitted under seal because the name of the witness appears in it. Please help us out further, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2171A, record by Borislav Stankov in B/C/S, under seal; Exhibit P2171.1, English translation under seal; Exhibit P2171B, forensic report in B/C/S under seal; Exhibit P2171B.1, English translation; Exhibit P3680, pseudonym sheet under seal; Exhibit D96, map marked by witness; Exhibit D97, B/C/S report 1st Corps command of 24th of June, 1993; Exhibit D97.1, English translation; Exhibit D98, on-site investigation report in B/C/S; Exhibit D98.1, English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I ask just for one reservation, that the document D97 admitted in evidence subject to us obtaining an official translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could a translation be provided by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. If we must, we shall do it as best we can to get the translation, so-called official translation. You know the time that is necessary. I believe that we can talk about months. But perhaps we could use the procedure that you have already suggested, that is, go through the Registry in order to speed up the whole matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The D97 is provisionally admitted and is finally admitted once a translation has been provided, and the Chamber orders that a translation will be made. So, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you can use the transcript in order to see how quickly it can be done. On the other hand, Mr. Stamp, I think if it is not there by tomorrow, it would not be of great concern to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next week would be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we still have another document on which we have to take a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not quite sure that I understood you well. Are you asking me to use the transcript to speed up the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the -- if the interpretation and translation unit knows that it's own specific request of the Chamber that a translation should be made, they should speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you take the transcript, make a copy of one page and yellow marker pen, that might be of some help. Then we still have P1517B, Madam Registrar. That is the colour version of the medical record of witness Mehonic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please,.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but C.1, may I just have a look at that to see whether -- yes. I think P1517C.1 cannot be admitted as it is now. Since a new translation leaving out those parts that do not appear in the original should be taken out from the translation. Is that correct, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed it is being done. I expect that to be available probably today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, with regard to this document, once again, and I am sorry if I am repeating myself, but we are very sorry. We think that this document which was obviously done in -- on two different occasions and that therefore, for this reason, the Defence would be very happy if this document were not admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, anything would have been added later on, for example, within the hospital, until now, we have seen this document in its original version as it has been given to the patient and as it has brought to this court by the witness who received it from the medical institution. Therefore, the objection against admission is denied. I think we then need a one or two-minute break and I would suggest that we do not leave the courtroom. A break necessary for the technicians to adjust the microphones to the testimony to be given by the next expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the interim, Mr. President and Your Honours, I respectfully ask to be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the technicians tell me whether they need another test or whether we could continue? We can continue. Mr. Ierace, is my understanding right that you would now call Mr. Donia an expert and that you'll just, I would say, on formality grounds, you would examine him in chief and then the expert being cross-examined by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's so, Mr. President and at some convenient point to you I would seek to tender the translation of a document, a translation that was requested during the evidence of Habib Trto. I think about two weeks ago coincidentally, it seems to indicate a turn around time of two weeks for fresh translations. Perhaps that could be done now or at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that could be done at a later point but perhaps you could give a copy to the registry so that we could see the translation before giving a decision on the admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President and might I point out that the entire document has been translated, not just the page in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another oral decision to make. The Prosecution has requested that the statement of a deceased witness - his name is Bajram Sopi - would be admitted into evidence. Meanwhile, the Defence has responded to that request and the Prosecution has asked leave to respond to the response. That leave is granted, and since the request for leave to respond was already accompanied by the response itself, we will proceed. But leave is granted. Then, would you, Mr. Usher, could you please assist Mr. Ierace in escorting the expert into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst he is being brought into the court, might I inform you that the supporting material is presently being collated -- excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the open source material, rather, is in the process of being collated, but in the meantime the balance of the material is available for the Bench at your convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we were informed about that. We were a bit surprised because it has been filed so it is available to the Bench. The only question we answered whether they should be submitted as a whole together with the report, but I do understand that full copies have been made again, which would not have been necessary as far as we are concerned, unless there is anything extra in the present copies compared to the copies filed before. If that would be so, then of course we would need a full new set and we would like to know what has been added. I can imagine that newspapers articles that you found or whatever would have been added. But if it is the same, well, I am afraid that this has been a loss of a lot of copying capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the open source material which has been requested by the Defence would become part of the Prosecution's tender, that is the newspapers articles, the audiotape speech by Radovan Karadzic, and certain other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so there has been some extras and then we will see how to do it, whether we return our copies or whether they will be destroyed, because we have copies until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It might be more convenient that there be a supplementary volume with that material together with the audiotape and also some video material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's perhaps the best way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please lead the expert witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The French booth asks you to slow down, and the same goes to Mr. Ierace, so they could better understand, better follow, and therefore, produce and perform better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace and I have the same problems now and then speaking the same language. Mr. Donia, I presume, Mr. Donia, before giving testimony before this Chamber, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, and the text will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Donia. I just like to inform you that your report has been filed. That means that parties and Chamber have read your report. And the procedural order is that you will be very briefly examined by the Prosecution, who called you as a witness, but then the main reason for your presence here is that the Defence has asked to have the opportunity to cross-examine you. So that we will start soon. Mr. Ierace, may I first give you the opportunity to examine Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Robert J. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown a copy of P3683, only the report, not the supporting materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Mr. Ierace, when you say "just the report," you mean the appendixes included and the footnotes so that means 30 pages of report -- no, 31 pages of -- no, 30 -- no. I have to apologise. I have a report of 25 pages, including footnotes, and I have three appendages: A personal curriculum vitae of Mr. Robert Donia and table one and map one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. There are some colour copies of the map available. If they could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: To be included as part of this Exhibit, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The Defence already has a copy, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said 33 pages. I had forgotten about the front page, so that makes 34. Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you have before you a report which bears your signature and the date the 25th of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the report titled "The Siege of Sarajevo, a Background Report?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please turn to Appendix A.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Appendix A, are have you set out some aspects of your personal history together with your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please go to page one of the curriculum vitae, that is the following page, number 28.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By way of addition to that document, is there a recent affiliation that should be added?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. Under "current affiliations" can be added an honorary appointment as Professor of History, the University of Sarajevo Philosophical Faculty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 30, under the heading "expert witness testimony," I think you list trials in this Tribunal in which you have given evidence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you also presently in the process of giving evidence in a trial of the Prosecutor and Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have no further questions in chief, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to make the following comment: Exceptionally, we will have to have much more time and we thank you for that in advance, than just a couple of minutes on the part of the Prosecution. Considering that we have decided this task, I will be asking some general questions and my colleague, Ms. Pilipovic, is going to deal with issues having to do with the footnotes. Having said that, we are now ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you consider yourself to be an expert historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, a historian with expertise in the history of the former Yugoslavia in the 19th and 20th centuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we move on any further, would you agree with the Defence in general that if we wish to understand certain events in the former Yugoslavia, we can't restrict ourselves to looking into the history of the period that you have just mentioned, that is to say the 19th and the 20th century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would nevertheless consider, and that is my understanding of the situation, that you are a specialist for the contemporary history or, more specifically, the two centuries that you have referred in relation to this geographical area in particular.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, before we move on to purely historical matters, I would like you to tell us a bit about yourself, about your training, your so-called academic achievement and your professional career. What was your last job, could you tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are several questions there. My -- to answer your last question first, I currently hold the three appointments indicated at the beginning of my CV. Prior to 1998, from 1981 to 1998, I was employed by the investment firm of Merrill Lynch and worked for Merrill Lynch in matters unrelated to the former Yugoslavia or south-east Europe. To your question regarding --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I believe there was just one question, the one that you have just answered, so I would like to interrupt you here, if you don't mind. According to the transcript, apparently we have a problem with figures. No, no. It is fine. Thank you very much. You have just mentioned that during two decades, basically, you had a completely different job. You worked for Merrill Lynch, the financial company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your title, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Resident Vice President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object on the basis of relevance. His employment at Merrill Lynch has nothing to do with his expertise for which he's called in this case. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you explain to us what the relevance of your question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I am coming to my point. What I would like to know is what exactly the academic career of the witness has been and, of course, now I have to reveal my purpose. And I would just like to know whether for the entire duration of that period, the witness had the opportunity to dwell on matters that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. President, your question was what post the expert held in Merrill Lynch, and I think the objection was about the relevance of that specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But you and I know that somebody who is just an employee in a big hierarchy, generally speaking, has more time off than person who is very high up and needs to concentrate a great deal on the job. But, basically, it has been taken out of my hands now. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may continue, but where Mr. Donia found his time to concentrate on other issues than Merrill Lynch would, in the view of this Chamber, not be relevant enough to be asked to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in the course of that period, did you dedicate all of your time to your employer, that is to say, the Merrill Lynch company?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Virtually all of my time, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you tell us or remind us about when you obtained your degree as a historian and at what university?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I obtained my undergraduate degree at Hope College in Holland, Michigan, in 1967. It was a degree in history. In 1974, I received a master's degree from the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, Michigan, and in 1976, received a Ph.D. in history from the University of Michigan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you be so kind as to tell us what the topic of your thesis was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I don't want to interrupt but the last question and then the new question, is there any -- do you want to check what is in the report or is there any reason to believe that it is not. I mean, I read the last answer which seems to certify you on page 31 and unless there is any reason to believe that -- of course, if that is your -- if that is your issue, than please proceed, but if it is just to have confirmed what is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have read the report, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you just very briefly remind us of what exactly your thesis was all about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The topic of my doctoral thesis was the political and social life of the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1878 until 1908.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are a specialist in what is called the "K und K" administration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That was the subject of my dissertation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when had you been appointed at the university of Sarajevo, the philosophy faculty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Within the past month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, previously, did you at any time hold a post which would be comparable to that of a lecturer, what is normally referred to as an ordinary professor, in French, a lecturer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I was an assistant professor of history to use the American academic term. At the Ohio State University, Lima Campus, from January 1978 until January 1981. In addition I was a visiting professor of history at the University of Oregon until the late spring of 1981. That was my last academic appointment prior to going to work for Merrill Lynch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly if I said that you were not a lecturer, a regular in-house lecturer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not familiar, unfortunately, with the French terminology or academic system. These were full-time academic appointments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in charge of a university department?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. You do not hold a chair, you are not a head of a department at any university at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. Witness, you have talked to us or rather you mentioned in the report which is been mentioned right now, the existence of a foundation and I believe the name of that foundation is Donia Vakuf. I do hope that I am pronouncing the name correctly. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if we understand what "Donia" means, could you tell us briefly what the word "Vakuf" stands for and, also, has it been taken from Arabic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Donia Vakuf Foundation took its name from the Donji Vakuf municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The term "Vakuf" is the Serbo-Croatian term, which is a slightly different form of the Arabic word "Waqaf" that refers to an Islamic foundation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us if you know it - I suppose you do know - what exactly the term that you have just used in Arabic means. "Waqaf," I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Waqaf is a piece of property, whether it is a shop or a piece of agricultural land or other earning asset, that is devoted to the maintenance of a particular religious, educational or cultural institution. It's therefore an endowment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it is a fund, if my understanding is correct, which is meant to fund certain types of work or certain activities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what is your role within the foundation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am the president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you also one of the founding members or the founding member?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I was one of the founding members, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. Witness, could we be told who provides the necessary funding for the functioning of this foundation, who are the donors?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the donor has been my family. This is a family foundation Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with the appropriate limitations under U.S. tax laws.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are saying the donor, and you are using the singular. So there is just one donor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I am going to ask is this: Are you getting paid as president?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. Witness, do you know - and you should know - whether this foundation has been involved on the spot in Bosnia-Herzegovina with reference to the carrying out of any projects?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether that foundation was involved in any religious or para-religious projects. When I say para-religious, what I mean is Islamic schools.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, it has not been.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has the foundation in any way at all been involved in projects involving Koranic schools?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No. The schools that have principally received the donations have been the University of Michigan and St. Lawrence University, both in the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the projects implemented by the foundation on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if there are any?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The projects that have been carried out on territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina have been in fact carried out by the University of Michigan and St. Lawrence University. The first project was the preparation of a bibliography of those items destroyed in the bombing of the library, National University Library of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in August of 1991 -- 92, that are in the possession of the University of Michigan libraries. In addition, the donations of the foundation have gone to support the project of General Divjak. I think the project is called "Children of Bosnia," and in support of various publication activities of the Intitute for History in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Those are the primary projects that have been supported. The University of Michigan project resulted in a the creation of a website which was called Cuprija, which is "bridge," and I think that some of the results of that review were placed on the website and done in conjunction with Bosnian members of the faculty at the University of Sarajevo and the National and University Library.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Let me now move on to another series of questions. You have indicated to us that in order to gain an understanding on what could have happened in the former Yugoslavia, one has to take a broader historic view and not just the contemporary period; do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The question I am going to ask you will go back in time because we have read some of your writings and you yourself are referring to that particular period. Could you just simply, and this is of importance to the Defence, tell us, where the line of rupture was following what is normally called the Great Schism?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There was no single line - geographic line that could divide those two places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the area was?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The area extended all the way from northern Russia throughout Europe, south-eastern Europe, down to the area of the Mediterranean Sea.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel repeat because we didn't hear. The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the English translators have asked Mr. Piletta-Zanin to repeat the question because they did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that include Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Did what include Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This area that we are referring to at the moment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you indicate as of when, if you know it, what is normally called the Glagolitic alphabet was used?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know precisely what, the date or the period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give us a century?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Before the -- it was certainly in use before the 12th century.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can one consider that with the adoption of Glagolitic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please speak into the microphone? Closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not sure if you're listening on the English channel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm listening into live channel at this moment, so I do not hear any translation. Whoever could assist me in warning me if the interpreters are having some problems, but I don't know what the problem is. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the request is whether you would come a bit closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to get hurt, but I'll do it with pleasure. [In English] Our profession is not without risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me continue and I do apologise, is it correct to consider that with the adoption of the fee -- of Glagolitic language, there is an overlap between the Latin world and the other?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the name of Mr. Brodel?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I have to check the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't know exactly when you would like to have a break. Perhaps this would be the appropriate moment. Perhaps we could take the break now because it is almost a quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn, if you would otherwise touch a new subject. We will adjourn, Mr. Donia, usually for half an hour, so we will resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.17 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. However, before I begin, I merely like to see something but it seems that the interpreters booth at times cannot hear me and therefore, if I may, I like to check with the booths to see if they hear -- if they can hear me, depending on the different booths. I don't know if the English booth can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can, even though I have to keep the volume up to the maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English booth answered it is better, even though we have to keep the volume up.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The answer is on the English channel, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you for this information. I do appreciate it. [Interpretation] And I was about to switch to the English channel. I believe it is now better. I will now test the second microphone. Can the English booth hear me better now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Not really. It is about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which of the two microphones seems to you better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The problem is that we have to keep the volume at the maximum level and therefore we now can hear well, but when the counsel turns away from the microphones, then we have no possibilities of putting up the volume further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is workable for the moment, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As long as the counsel speaks into the microphone rather than away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there is a specific request that you speak into the microphone, and perhaps overnight the technicians could see why it is that the interpreter booth hardly can hear Mr. Piletta-Zanin when I always hear him. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. I shall try to do what I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we shall now resume. Now that we have solved this minor technical problem and I am on the English channel and I hope that it will work. Very well. I'd like to go back in particular to your report and to the period of time which has to do with the K and K administration, the Austro-Hungarian administration in Bosnia. You speak about the Black Hand. You mentioned the Black Hand. Did you do it of your own volition? I mean, you did not mention the Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was it of your own choice? Did you do that on purpose?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was of my own choice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: My report begins with the period 1990. This is a reference to something that happened or was relevant to the history of the region some 75 years previous to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. But we see that in these proceedings there are often historical references and I'd like you to tell us now, what is generally meant by the word "Chetnik?"

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The Chetnik term applies to groups of Serbian volunteers and bandits who fought against the Ottoman administration in the late Ottoman years and in the Balkan Wars. It was further used by the coalition of groups headed by General Draza Mihailovic. In the Second World War. A group of rebels or resistance fighters who were formed from remnants of the Royal Yugoslav Army -- pardon me. And subsequently came to collaborate with the Germans at times and were ultimately defeated by the partisans in World War II. In the 1990s, it was revived by some Serbian political leaders of ultra-nationalist orientation to describe their paramilitary groups and also was used in many cases by people who were under attack by Bosnian Serb forces to describe the forces attacking them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. I heard the word "general" and the name, and I believe that he was a royalist that you mentioned. But unfortunately the name did not appear in the transcript. So could you please repeat the name of that general?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes. General Draza Mihailovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Overnight these names are corrected, so it is not necessary to have the witness to repeat names again and again. It was clearly audible in -- must be clearly audible on the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were telling us about a period covering a relatively long chronologically period of time. Does the name "Amendola" ring any bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, not -- no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does the 16th of April, 1994, ring any bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does the name of Richard Davis ring any bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Mr. Richard Davis is your colleague?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Richard Davis that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us if this is 16th of April, 1944 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The second time that "44" appears on the transcript as "94." Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am talking about 1944, 4-4. The 16th of April wasn't -- didn't the Allied Forces, did the Allies bomb Belgrade on that date?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does Arthur Harris, is that a name that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the name "Spatz"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And what about Dresden, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Dresden is a town in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the 13th and 14th of February, 1945, ring any bell with you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Not particularly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I tell you that during -- that on those two days, the Allied Air Force commanded by Arthur Harris launched two air raids against Dresden, would you agree with me that that is a fact of history?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this question and, indeed, the previous questions over the last three minutes or so, on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, could you please explain to us the relevance, but may I remind you if you ask about certain dates or certain persons of whom the witness says that it doesn't -- that do not ring a bell with him, that we have no idea of what it is about unless you explain it to us. But on the latter part, you started to do so. Nevertheless, it, we understand that it has got something to do with your representation, and so please could you tell us the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Very well. The relevance is as follows: The Prosecution bases its position on the existence of a campaign, on the existence of a campaign which was supposedly, if not ordered, then accepted by General Galic, who went along with it, and which resulted in a certain number of deaths. The Defence challenges the existence of such a campaign and the number of dead. What the Defence wishes to arrive at is to establish with this witness who is an expert, as he told us, on the modern period, that is the preceding century and the 19th century, because that not only a few years ago but some decades ago there were also major bombings, and so that on the basis of that, we could then eventually take all the necessary decisions. This person was called by the Prosecution as an expert historian, and I believe the Defence is entitled to examine what happened in history a few decades back and a few miles away from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, does "Bomber Harris" or the expression, the term, "Bomber Harris," are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, as a historian expert in the 20th century history, are you telling us that you never heard mentioned either General Spatz nor Bomber Harris?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not aware of where Mr. Donia has said that he was an expert in 20th century history. He has referred to the modern period in the Balkans. Perhaps Mr. Piletta-Zanin can take us back to what is the foundation for that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase it, if I may. If I may, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, didn't you sometime ago tell us that your area concerned the 19th and the 20th century, that you specialised in those two centuries?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I indicated I consider my specialty to be the lands of the former Yugoslavia in the 19th and 20th centuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Would it be possible to study the history of that period whilst isolating artificially a particular territory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is very possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are telling me that it is possible to study the history of a region without at the same time studying what went around that territory at that same time, is that it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It is possible and it is done all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, I will take note of that. You told me a moment ago that you were familiar with the word "Dresden," which is the name of a city. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know if towards the end of the war, the World War II, do you know -- are you aware of massive bombing of Dresden towards the end of the war and that the city was practically razed to the ground as a result?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I am saying that let us assume, and I know that it was the 13th or 14th of February, 1945; are you aware of the number of victims which the historians generally attributed to that particular bombing, to that particular air raids?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I give you the figure of some 300.000 victims, the death would be the ultimate magnitude and that they were mostly civilians, would that jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know what the casualty figures were from the bombing, and I can't speculate without some enquiry into the opinions of those who studied that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to -- Witness, does the name of "Little Boy," ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about "Fat Man"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does "Anola" or "Enola" mean anything to you, that is female first name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: As a female first name, I am not certain -- that rings no bell. If you're referring to the Enola Gay as an airplane, that was the name given to an airplane in World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that plane?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: It was the plane that carried an atomic bomb that was dropped on, I believe it was Hiroshima, in 1945.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is correct. Thank you for that answer. And the bomb was called "Little Boy." Does it now ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I appreciate the decision that you made a few minutes ago in relation to the line of questioning, but this quiz that my learned colleague is engaging is, in my respectful submission, of no assistance. It is premised, having regard to my learned colleague's last answer, it seems, on the presumption that the Prosecution case is that the accused in this case sought to kill as many civilians as possible. Mr. President, it should be apparent from the Prosecution pre-trial brief that, whatever his orders were, that is not what he intended to do, that is, he did not intend to destroy the city, in the Prosecution case. Mr. President, the Prosecution has a time limit on it to present its case, and in my respectful submission, the Defence bears some responsibility of limiting its questions to matters which are relevant and approaching those matters in an efficient way, rather than playing a quiz with the witness and then try to string together the last groups of 10 answers into one final question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you want to raise a certain issue, please come to the point and no quizzes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so. But before that, will you allow me a comment, please. And it has to do with the French transcript, which I am looking from the corner of my eye now, and this seems to be important: "Mr. Galic has never intended to kill as many witnesses as possible," and that is what came out on the French booth. I would really like that to be corrected, with or without a quiz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us resume. Witness, how many civilian victims were there after that first bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I maintain my objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you want to raise an issue of comparison with historic events which caused a great number of casualties. There is no problem with that. But it is of no use whether, unless it is in dispute between the parties, whether it is 100.000, 200.000, a million, or 25.000. Make your point, ask questions about what -- the issue you want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so, Mr. President. I will ask this question:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the figure -- does the figure of 180.000 victims seem acceptable to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know the number of victims and I can't speculate without consulting some source of those who do know. Certainly, this order of magnitude is a reasonable one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the chief of the Pacific Air Force at the time, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. General Spatz was even brought to justice?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the signature was -- of the person who signed that, who ordered that bombing, and that was, if I am correct, President Truman, was he ever subject to any kind of Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object again to this line of questioning. It is of no assistance, in my respectful submission, to equate the crimes that are alleged to have been committed to General Galic to these historical events. It is of no assistance in determining whether or not this accused is guilty of the crimes with which he is charged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is a two-tiered matter. There is the General Galic's responsibility within an alleged campaign and there are historical examples of true massacres of civilians for -- and the Defence would like to know, whether yes or no, historically speaking certain positions were taken by the international community. And we would like to hear the answer to that and we would like it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But massacres in the -- I would say in the recent past which caused huge numbers of casualties, that remained not prosecuted, not punished, is that in dispute between the parties? It is not in dispute. So it is not an issue at this moment. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I am going to come back to a period that you are no doubt more familiar with. It is the decade which preceded the 1990s in Yugoslavia and Europe. Is it correct that you consider yourself to be a specialist of both this particular period and this particular region?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, let us place all this within context, properly. In order to do that, could you confirm that the fall of the Berlin Wall happened in 1989?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Can you confirm that the fall of Mr. Ceausescu at the end of that year and he was executed in 1999 -- 1990?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I believe he was executed at the end of 1989 but, well, maybe it is 1990. Witness, could we, as a consequence, consider that the end of the 1980s, in as far as Yugoslavia was concerned, it was formally the last communist state in Europe?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that is the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to move on to an easier question. I believe that you were also interested in the economic situation in Yugoslavia with regard to that specific period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, have you looked at the developments in the GDP in Yugoslavia of that time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, not specifically at the GDP numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Generally speaking, could you confirm that during that particular period, the one that we are referring to now, Yugoslavia was faced with worsening economic crisis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you confirm that that was the case, Witness, for all of the republics, all of the six republics which made up former Yugoslavia; it was more serious for some and less for the others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- could we say that in that period former Yugoslavia was moving towards general impoverishment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. Witness, in the course of that period, have you had any information at all about the existence of any economic assistance, either from Europe, the European Community, that is, or from the U.S., the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There were many loans extended and development grants made from principally the U.S., but also the European Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true to consider that by the end of the 1980s that assistance was cut drastically?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, toward the very end of the 1980s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a question I am putting to a historian, that is to say, an expert. Well, do you think in view of the overall situation that you are familiar with, that this restriction or decrease in aid could have lead to certain social movements or events such as the ones we are discussing today?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think it was a minor factor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us why, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The much more deep cause of the economic crisis and consequent social movements were the internal situation within Yugoslavia, the rapid inflation, the political crisis, and the general deterioration of productivity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the extent that there had been an overall deterioration of production, wasn't it then obvious that that situation would necessarily lead to a clear crisis between various components of the Yugoslav nation or the Yugoslav state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I don't think it was inevitable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you followed the developments whereby at a certain point what is normally referred to as Yugoslav secession took place?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not quite clear what you mean by "Yugoslav secession or succession."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. What I meant by secession, I meant the point of time when different republics, starting from Slovenia, started to secede, legally separate or practically separate, from the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I did follow that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you examined the positions of all the various protagonists within Europe in relation to this matter of international recognition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have not examined the position of all protagonists, but the primary ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, Witness, examined the position of the main protagonists, which were Germany on the one hand, the newly united Germany on the one hand and France on the other hand?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for this answer. Perhaps the name Jacques Attali tells you something?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to my previous question.
