As far as you know, Witness, is it correct that the French position, as expressed by President Francois Mitterand at the time, was one of urgent waiting - if I may use this term - "urgent waiting" without proceeding to whatever sort of immediate international recognition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: That is a reasonably accurate characterisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that reply, Witness. This is not a quiz. But do you know for what reason basically the French Presidency and the French Cabinet did not wish to proceed too rapidly in the direction of that international recognition?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You are speaking recognition of the independence of Slovenia and Croatia. I think, for their position, they wished to act as part of the European Community and wished to avoid any direct involvement on their own in the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Is that -- is it correct that we are talking about the formal application, but, Witness, don't you think that there was some fundamental reasons due to which France, in other words the French Presidency, wished to put a break in this mechanism, which, as we know, has led to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think I have just identified what I understand to be France's position, and I'm sure there are other reasons that went into its particular role in the crisis. But those would be the primary ones I would identify.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to come back to this question. Thank you. Is it not correct that, on the other hand, the other partner from the Franco-German Acts, Germany, that is, that they wish to rather speed up the process of legal disintegration?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not -- I wouldn't agree with your characterization that they wished to accelerate the process of legal disintegration. The German government did, in fact, favour recognition, and acted to recognise the independence of Slovenia and Croatia in advance of [Realtime transcript read in error "and"] the European Community decision in December 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In December 1991, you are certain of your date there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: The recognition announcement was made -- of the European Community -- was made in January of 1992 and I believe the German announcement of its intent to recognise was December 19 or 21. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I notice there are some words missing from the English transcript. I don't know whether they would have been caught by the evening review. Page 48, line 17, after Croatia, I think the words "in advance of," should be inserted before the European decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what my recollection is as well. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please look at line 17 of page 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] Which line, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 17. It reads: "enacted to recognise the independence of Slovenia and Croatia in advance or of the European decision in December 1991." Is that your recollection, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I believe so, but we could turn to the witness and insert his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether the Germans wished to speed up, I just briefly mention now, that your answer, the German government did in fact favour recognition and acted to recognise the independence of Slovenia and Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In advance of the European Community decision and the date of December 1991 pertains to the German decision, the German act, not the European Community decision which was subsequent to January, 15th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You clarified that in your later answers. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To come back to this specific point once again, is it not true, Witness, that the German government had almost given an ultimatum to the European Community by saying that if the Community did not recognise, we are going to recognise these new states on our own independently. Does it remind you of anything?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it reminds me that specifically the German government announced its intent to recognise in advance of the conclusions of the Badinter Commission, which were not reached until early January and announced on 15 January. Whether it issued an ultimatum to the European Community, I am not aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply, Witness. You are at the moment an honorary professor at the University of Sarajevo, that's my understanding; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you are at the philosophy faculty, I believe that, in fact, it also includes the history department?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this reply. Since you were appointed by the authorities, we might be led to think that you have good connections in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not too sure what the question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe, I mean that you have good connections in Sarajevo since you are in a way perhaps an employee of the University of Sarajevo, you teach there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is still not a question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. You told the witness what you believe to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I do not teach there. This, I emphasise, was an honorary designation. I understand it to involve no work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you had any stays -- have you visited Bosnia-Herzegovina recently?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I last visited in February of this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 2002 then?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You visited Sarajevo in your capacity as a historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have access to the press published in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, most of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you can read Serbian perfectly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, not perfectly, but well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether as a consequence as a poorer reader -- well, that's not exactly what I meant to say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Says Mr. Piletta-Zanin, correcting the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you are barely capable to read the local newspapers, but even so, do you feel you can gain access to certain information in relation to some certain massacres?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't specifically know. I'd have to know specifically what you mean in order to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the local newspapers ever referred to the so-called Kazani graves?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, have you yourself ever found any reference at all to the so-called Kazani mass grave?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't understand your reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question on the basis of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if you have difficulty explaining it to us in the presence of the witness, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no difficulty whatsoever in explaining it you because I believe the witness is completely competent pertaining to all matters of history. First of all, we need to put things into perspective and we must try to find out whether there could have been any mechanisms which at a certain point might have triggered off such and such an attack. It may well happen that a massacre happened at a certain part, logically could have provoked a given reaction on the part of the other party. So it is important for us to find out what could have happened at a given point in time, and we even have specific, precise dates here. I am astonished that the Prosecution seems to be surprised because they, themselves, have submitted the document that I am referring to. So I'm just trying to figure out if the witness is familiar with those events which happened at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, but I think at the very moment you could come quicker to the point. We don't have any objection, but if you first ask whether he has read it in the newspapers, then whether he heard it on the radio, then whether he heard it on television -- I assume that you want to come to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Straight away. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether there had been a massacre in connection with the so-called Kazani grave whereby several thousands or perhaps hundreds of dead bodies, Serb bodies, were buried?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One last point. Since you have followed this particular period in history very closely, unfortunately, do you know whether in this particular period that we are looking at, 1992, 1993 and 1994, the media were easily accessible, the information from the media was easily accessible in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Accessible to whom?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your average man in the street.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: To the average man in the street in Sarajevo, in general, during this period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions at this stage and it is my colleague, Mrs. Pilipovic, who is going to continue, unless the break is approaching.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, as a person who has studied history for a long time - I can see that you have got your doctorate in history as well - can you agree with me if I say that historians always keep one unpleasant fact in mind, that is to say, that factual truth can never be establish with any degree of certainty and that, in some instances, it is impossible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do tell us -- well, since you have answered no, but you do say that certain periods in history may be studied on the basis of facts referred to by historians, that they can be studied and statements can be made with a great deal of certainty?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are some periods about which one can have greater certainty than other periods. In general, one can establish greater certainty in the modern period than in the early modern or ancient periods. But sometimes there are islands of mystery in the modern period as well. I think it depends on the fact base, the documentation available, how close one can approach determining what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you tell us how come you take an interest in General Galic's case?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have a long-standing interest in Sarajevo, the city and the area, and began about two years ago to prepare a study of the history of the city. So consequently my interest in the city's past, into the dark, faraway Ottoman period and in the more modern period has always been strong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically with regard to your expert report, can you tell us what was your task specifically? Rather, what were you told to cover?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I was asked to prepare a background report to the events of the period of the indictment which pertain to the immediate post-election time from November 1990 until the summer of 1992. I was asked to do that in ten pages, which you and Your Honours will recognise, I exceeded, but tried to do within a very limited and as concise as possible form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in your expert report, you examined the period of 1990, 1991, and 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Until the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you asked to do that as a historian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you have your -- you have a copy of your report before you, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I'll ask you more specific questions emanating from your report, I would like to ask you to tell us, and this has to be with the substance of your report: In view of what you say on -- of your report which covers 28 pages, together with footnotes -- no, sorry, 23 pages, and footnotes are included there, is that the contents of your report and are the footnotes, do the footnotes make a part of your report? That is, can we see them as an integral part of your part, as part and parcel of your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your report, you also speak about some natural features of the city of Sarajevo. Could you tell us what were the sources on which your conclusions were based in those parts where we speak about characteristics of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the region of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Can you be specific about what section you are looking at?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I am looking at page three of your report. And there in passage three, "The city extended westward several kilometres as skyscrapers were built in a valley and on the hills around the old city, around Stari Grad, and then extending further, the city also encompassed several rural areas." Mr. Donia, I apologise, it is page three of the translation. I do not have the original version. Perhaps my colleague has it and can help me to make it more efficient. It is right underneath the title "The Nationalists Replace Communists." The next passage when you refer to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's on the first page. The third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. It is on the first text page of the report. And I have a footnote there, but this is, I mean, from personal observation, the awareness of the city's expansive area known as Sarajevsko Polje, to the west and south and, to some degree, north of the downtown area, principally west of the downtown area. And there are numerous studies of the building of the urban area or urban residential areas to the west. I didn't cite any particular one because it seemed to me there was no particular contention about that simple characterization.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that when I asked you what sources that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. used, that those were your personal observations; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, before you did this report, how often did you visit Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Some 20, 25 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when was that? Can you give us the time frame, that is up to 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I visited first in 1965, was there several times during the 1970s, and once in 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us -- you have answered, you have told me what was your task. Can you now tell us how much time did you spend preparing your report, your opinion, including the time that you used for the preparation of your expert report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: About 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when did you start work on your expert report or rather when were you asked to do that? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe in November of 2001.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your expert report you speak about the regionalisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Can you tell us again, what were the sources that underpin your conclusions about these social and economic causes of the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the eve of the war?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think that's two questions. The regionalisation campaign had little to do with the second part of the question, which is the economic and social sources of the crisis. So, if I can answer the second part of your question first, the late 1980s brought severe inflation and an effort to reduce this inflation through the reforms of Ante Markovic. And those were basically unsuccessful and produced a drastic drop in productivity and living standards that contributed, I think, substantially to the crisis, the economic crisis and the subsequent political movements that arose. Regionalisation, as I explained in the paper, was a term used to describe the SDS campaign, to create one party, single nationality control over certain territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And cited some of those factors --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we shall come to that later. My question was: What sources did you use in preparing your report, in preparing this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have examined the periodical press from Banja Luka, Sarajevo and in some other cases other publications and the minutes of the SDS assembly sessions and certain other documents pertaining to the regionalisation campaign, which were in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you prepared your expert report and that the source of the documents was the documentation that you received from the Prosecutor's office and the press; is that it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I think I should certainly state that I spent considerable time prior to the time that I entered in the preparation of this report in the study of the city of Sarajevo in the 20th century and consequently have looked at a wide variety of documents, periodical press, local documents over a century or more of time. So, I would add that there is some, let's say general, preparation which is behind the specific report that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us this: In your expert report, there is a chapter entitled "The Military Preparations and the Road to War." Could you tell us what were the sources that you used for your conclusions on the military aspects of the crisis and the armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think the specific sources are cited in footnotes. There are -- there is ample documentation on the role of -- I have to go kind of sentence by sentence, section by section. There is substantial documentation on the role of the SDA-sponsored military groups that is in published form: Interviews in the periodic press, a couple of memoirs. The information on the Croatian paramilitary group is derived from periodic press information, from a series of books written about the Yugoslav crisis and subsequent dissolution of Yugoslavia. I can go and give you further information, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. At some point, speaking about the literature you said you also used some memoirs. Could you tell us whose, that is, whose book was it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, I have made reference to a number of memoirs, made reference to the memoir-istic recollections of General Kukanjac, to the memoirs of General Kadijevic, also referred to the -- although not cited here -- the memoirs of General Siber, of Mr. Jovic, which is a diary in memoir form. I've looked at the memoirs of General Halilovic and General Efendic. I've looked at the memoir literature, perhaps not all of it, but a number of those works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When preparing your report, did you also visit Republika Srpska and did you use literature -- or were the documents in Republika Srpska also the source for your report -- or rather the first question, have you ever visited Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague has changed the wording of the question, by now I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, when preparing your expert report, did you use documents from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have conducted some interviews in Republika Srpska and used documents from the territory that is now part of Republika Srpska. I have not referenced those documents while in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which were those documents even though there are no references to them, but they nevertheless helped you write this report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I must take exception, there are references to them throughout the report. These are minutes of the SDS -- I am sorry, the assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina; the newspaper Glas in Banja Luka. I have also looked at but not referenced here the minutes of the meetings of the Bosnian Krajina Assembly, and have, I believe, here cited as well the newspaper that was put out initially in Sarajevo and then, I believe, moved to Pale, which was the Javnost, the publication of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if you could find a suitable moment within the next one or two minutes to give us an opportunity to have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, by analysing the documents that you used for your expert report, and by making reference to the footnotes, can we agree that 80 per cent of your material came from the newspaper Oslobodenje, when it comes to the press, and two articles carried by Banja Luka Glas, but that one can conclude that it was principally Oslobodenje, a paper which is published in Sarajevo and Slobodna Bosna, also published in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, can you confirm that you also used other printed press, but did not mention it in the footnotes? Is that what you want to tell us?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I believe your question was: Could I confirm that 80 per cent of the citations were from Oslobodenje. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm it to us that it was by and large Oslobodenje that you used, that it was your chief source?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Oslobodenje is an important source for this paper, yes. It is one of several important sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this would be a convenient time for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. We will adjourn until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 5.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before we resume cross-examination, I would be grateful if my learned colleagues could indicate whether they expect the cross-examination will last all of tomorrow. That will assist in arranging for the attendance of the next witness, if that's required before Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question is, as a matter of fact whether the any time remain tomorrow to call any -- could you give us an indication, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that yes, my cross-examination would take the whole of tomorrow. Because of the document that we were given yesterday and today, we simply cannot be all that efficient. I really do not know what else we shall be using and what we shall be showing to the witness because it was only yesterday that I was given documents and tapes, and especially documents with footnotes. That is it. We simply received it only yesterday. Otherwise, perhaps it would have been more efficient, but I shall do my best not to go beyond -- not to ask any questions beyond the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, Mr. Ierace, are there any witnesses available, if you would have some remaining time tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there was a witness that we would have called before Mr. Donia and he is waiting. But he understood that he may not be required before -- until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, to send him back again, that is no option, I think. So let's try to use our time as efficiently as possible. You indicated you would need two days. So it is already a little bit less if you would finish by tomorrow. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your expert report, you addressed some military questions as well. Can you tell us if you are an expert on matters military, on military strategy and other military matters?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't consider myself an expert on military strategy or military matters, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to show the witness a conclusion. The Defence can read it and the witness can read it himself. It is a conclusion on page 15 of the translation, before the footnotes. It is six lines long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, the report will be admitted into evidence, I assume, so therefore it is not necessary to read. We have all read it and Mr. Donia has even written it. So ask him whatever questions you would like about the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you have before you your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 14 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you have your conclusion before you. Do you still stand by your conclusion that there was a siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you define the siege.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This was a military encirclement that controlled or prevented entry or egress from the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can you tell us on the basis of which sources did you establish that there was a siege of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Cited on page 12 of the English language report are assertions from General Mladic, the SDS President Karadzic, Trifko Radic and Dragan Kalinic, statements to that effect. There are certainly numerous other sources which speak to the limitation of movement into and out of the city and the fact that it was militarily encircled, but I think those are very plain indications from the -- some of the principle personalities that there was a siege and it was sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that from the documents that you got from the Prosecution and, specifically, when you mention these statements by General Mladic, by Mr. Radic and Mr. Kalenic, you are referring to the Serbian assembly held on the 12th of May 1990, is that it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: 12th of May, 1992. That is a transcript of the session of the Serbian assembly. The siege is also referred to in the documents of numerous visitors. I have cited, for example, Mr. Mazowiecki's visit and I've cited, of course, a number of the United Nations Security Council resolutions dealing with the siege. And also the conference of the -- the London conference notations regarding the international discussion of that by negotiators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I will go back to the questions which are related to the minutes of the session of the Serb assembly on the 12th of May, and I will ask you some questions about it. But apart from those minutes, I would just like to hear your assessment of these statements of people whom you mentioned a while ago who were present at this assembly. You also said that you used some other sources. Could you tell us which are those other sources, as you called them?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think I just gave them to you, the other sources that I cited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are saying that other documents that you quoted can also be found in the footnotes, the documents that you used in arriving at your conclusion that what one was dealing with was the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, we can agree that, apart from the documents that you referred to in your expert report, you did not use any other documents which would support your conclusion about the definition of the siege?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I referred to many other documents. I have not included them in the report. I have not provided a definition of the siege in the report, I just gave you my understanding of what a siege is. So the answer to your question, I think, is, no, we can't agree on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- you have just told us that you gave your view, which of those other documents that you used since we did not agree beforehand, apart from the documents that are indicated in the footnotes? Could you quote a book or a document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I've already indicated a substantial collection memoirs which I have consulted; the United Nations Commission of Experts; I have looked at numerous international press reports. I also had the experience myself of being in beseiged Sarajevo in July of 1994 and January of 1995. The documentary record on the siege, it seems to me, is extraordinarily rich, and virtually every visitor who came to Sarajevo in that period and wrote about it so reported.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you were in Sarajevo in 1993 and also 1994? Did I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Since my friend has rephrased the question, I don't object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is 1994 and 1995 we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as to say 1993 and 1994, but I accept -- I accept your statement that it was 1994 and 1995. And during your visits in Sarajevo, you told us that there were numerous documents and that supposedly includes your stay, but did you have -- did you have any opportunity to see military documents of the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I have seen a number of published documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which are the documents that you had the opportunity to see?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: There are some documents that were published in General Efendic's book, "Tko Ja Branio Sarajevo." And I believe, in the appendix to General Halilov's book, there are some published documents. There are -- I can't recall other works that I have seen these things in, but there are a number of those documents that have been published, some of them quite recently, in accounts by Bosnian army officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you are aware of the existence of the army of BH and the activities of the army of BH. Can you give us the names of military units holding positions in and around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: You have asked two questions there. Am I aware of the army of BH and some of its activities? Yes, I am. Could I give you names of military units' holding positions in and around Sarajevo? No, I can't give you a list of all positions that were held in and around Sarajevo. At one point, I know these came under the command of the 1st Corps of the Army of BH and that the -- I also am aware that the 15th of April, 1992 Presidency declaration put all units under a common command which at that time was designated, I believe, Territorial Defence, and subsequently became the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any information as to the number of armed soldiers? You have just told us that on the 15th of April, 1992, the Territorial Defence grew into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you have any information as to the type of the armaments that they had and how many armed soldiers were there in the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Let me just go back and characterise that statement. I think the way I gave it originally, on the 15th of April, 1992, all units were brought under a common command which at that time was the Territorial Defence. That force subsequently became or grew into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina formally in the summer of 1992, and I am not certain of the date. I do not know the total number of soldiers that were under arms of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in total, nor specifically in Sarajevo. It would number in the thousands in the case of Sarajevo, but I don't know beyond that, that I could characterise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the preparation of your expert report and the time when you were wording your conclusion, the one that we are talking about now, you said that you did not -- that you had not looked at the documents of the BH army, that your knowledge came from books written after the war, but did you also ever endeavour to consult some sources from the Serb side at the time when you were thinking about your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question. There is a loose connection between that question and the evidence the witness has recently given which causes me to submit that the question lacks any probative value. The witness has already indicated at some length what sources he used for that conclusion from the Serb side by referring my learned colleague back to page 12 of his report. Therefore, the question, in my respectful submission, lacks any probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, my questions refer to Mr. Donia's conclusion. We are talking about the siege, that is the conclusion that it was the siege of Sarajevo. In my question, so are of a more general nature at first, but now I am talking about the conclusion that is about the word, "siege," and I believe it is relevant for the Defence to get information because Mr. Donia has just told us that the army of BH was formed on the 15th of April 1992, that it grew out of the Territorial Defence, that he used certain documents and therefore my interest there rests with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, I do understand your explanation. It was not clear from your question. Do I understand that you want to ask the witness whether he has consulted any Serbian sources when reaching the conclusion that Sarajevo was sieged at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that was the purpose of my question, whether he had referred to any documents from the RS Army, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in reaching that conclusion, if that was the question, it was not the words of the question, then the objection is denied. You may answer the question, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask which question I am answering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I formulated it, I think "do I understand, I said that you, that is Ms. Pilipovic, want to ask the witness whether he has consulted any Serbian sources when reaching the conclusion that Sarajevo was siege at that time?" I think that is the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as I indicated earlier, I have cited Serbian sources in the first instance. These were statements, proclamations, speeches at the session of 12 May, 1992. I have also looked at the interviews with General Mladic and a book about him in which he has interviewed extensively which I think assist in that determination. But I would say for this report my citation is principally of Serbian sources and, principally, statements at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear some sounds, quite loud. I don't know where they come from. I don't hear them any more. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you said that when working on your report and reaching your conclusions in your expert report, you looked into no military documents from the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I did not make that statement. That's not an accurate characterisation of what I said. I indeed looked at numerous statements by the leadership of the army of Republika Srpska, specifically, General Mladic, and I would consider that a document of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Has the statement by General Mladic from the assembly of the 12th of May, 1992, and the part that you have quoted here, is something you consider proof and the document you reference that you used in order to reach your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you, in the course of your stay in Sarajevo, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the period of time between 1994 and 1995 ever interviewed General Mladic, have you ever talked to him?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in that period, have interviews with General Stanislav Galic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, when preparing your expert report, or in the period of time that you spent in Sarajevo, you said you were there in the 90s and 1994 and 1994, have you ever had the opportunity to meet or talk to Mr. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you are not a military expert, but in spite of that you deal with military matters and you draw conclusions. Can you agree with me that it is the realm, the area of competence of military experts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: What is the realm -- I am sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I told you that, as a Defence counsel, when reading through your report, I reached a conclusion or rather you, yourself, said you were not a military expert, but in spite of that we can both agree that you deal with military matters and you reach conclusions on those matters. Is it within your area of competence to look into military matters, to carry out analyses of the actions of military commanders and their statements? Can you agree with me that it is not within the realm of a historian but within the area of competence of a military expert?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. I think the role of a historian in a situation like this is to assess the military situation together with social, political, economic factors, and reach a general assessment of these matters as part of a broad and entire situation. And that inevitably leads one into military matters in the case of an armed conflict. I certainly would distinguish that between a military expert who would be trained in matters of tactics and strategy and particular weaponry and weaponry capability. Those are not matters that are my primary interest or concern, but I think that a military situation must be assessed as part of the broad context in which events occur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling us that, according to you, a military expert would be somebody who could carry out an analysis of a situation within a broader context, analysing military documents, referring to the period of time referred to here, with reference to General Stanislav Galic, and that that would be the appropriate person to come up with the real definition of siege of the city?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conclusion on page two after the term, "the army of the Republika Srpska," you said: "And the forces of the Bosnian Serbs under the command of Mladic and the leadership of Karadzic were vastly superior in power," et cetera. Is it a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Mladic's command and Karadzic leadership, do you make a distinction between the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and the forces under Mladic's command and Karadzic's leadership? Is my understanding correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. There seems to be some confusion about -- as to the reference to page two to which I do understand is line two of the conclusion. That is what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, did I make myself clear? Since your wording may be ambiguous to my mind, that is to say, it is not clear to me whether you made a distinction between the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and forces under Mladic's command and Karadzic's leadership?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In this sentence, I state that the Bosnian Serb forces were under Mladic's command and Karadzic's leadership, and that those forces enjoyed an overwhelming advantage in weaponry. I am aware that the statement that they are under Mladic's command is not the same as saying that they are under Karadzic's leadership, and I am certainly also aware that there was not always harmony prevailing between those two persons. But I think the general statement that the Bosnian Serb forces were under Mladic's command and Karadzic's leadership is valid and hardly requires a military specialist to reach that conclusion. And would certainly say that the overwhelming advantage in weaponry was evident to every observer at the time and is reflected in the host of not only press statements, but as reflected in the documents of the Republika Srpska as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what are those documents you are referring to? Are you referring to the documents you quote in your footnotes, or are there some other documents?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think I have indicated several times now that the documentation from the Republika Srpska -- Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina is replete with references to these things both at the session of 12 May and the 1995 50th session which address such matters. Those are documents of the Republika Srpska or whatever its iteration was known as at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. The Defence is in the possession of these documents and we will ask several questions in relation to those documents, but you are confirming once again that these are the documents that we are talking about. Once, you used the term documents and I thought you referred to something else. Do you, as a historian, have any data as to whether there was absolute unity between political and military authorities in the Muslim side, that is to say, the BH Army and the political leadership of the BH Army and the state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to the conflicts within the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Yes, there is. The memoirs of the Bosnian army commanders are made up in substantial measure of such conflicts. They pertain to a number of disputes about strategy and about leadership of the Bosnian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the fact that in 1993 and 1994 there were some -- there were some armed conflict in Sarajevo between commanders of different military units?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am aware that there was armed conflict between commanders, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that armed conflict between commanders spread and involved certain military formations?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, it is hard to characterise it beyond -- excuse me, beyond what I have. Did it spread, I don't know. It was at times widespread and I think that some of the conflicts came from different sources rather than a single disagreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the conflicts, the armed conflict within the BH Army involving different military formations were of a wider scope?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Wider than what? I referred to conflicts between commanders in, I think you asked me, about 1993, 1994. There were conflicts beyond those armed conflicts among commanders and their units in Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the consequences of such armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just told us that you do know of the existence of some such conflict. I am going to try to rephrase my question. Do you know anything about the nature of the consequences of such armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, they divided -- divided the Bosnian army in north-western Bosnia and resulted in some changes of command within the army in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about there being any armed conflict between military units within Sarajevo after those changes? What I mean, is within the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I am not too sure what period you refer to. I would only say that I am aware that there were conflicts among commanders. I could not give you precise dates of those conflicts, nor the particular players that were involved in them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to your conclusion about the siege. You have told us that they were superior in terms of artillery, the JNA was superior. Can you tell us in relation to what?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Relative to the fire power enjoyed by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you do know about the armaments and the weaponry of the BH army since you did say that the other side was superior?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: As I indicated in the accounts of the various commanders of the Bosnian army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there are constant references to the lack of weapons, lack of ammunition. These are echoed in the reports from the commission of experts. Throughout 1992 and early 1993, I cannot say I looked extensively at the documentation beyond this period that I have examined in the report, but in this period from April 1992 through the end of the summer of 1992, it seemed to have been the principal preoccupation of the Bosnian army to note their constant and repeated lack of heavy weapons of the type that the JNA and later BSA had in its possession.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to your conclusion and your expert report, you are saying that the Serb forces occasionally shelled the city, destroyed the religious and cultural heritage and deprived civilians of food, electricity, water, gas and transport. Can you tell us what sort of data or what statements you used and referred to in order to arrive at the conclusion that the civilian population was deprived of electricity, water, fuel, and transport. Let me clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: My friend as cross-examined the witness as to the sources of information for his conclusion that the Bosnian Serb army had an advantage in terms of armaments. There has been no issue about that prior to this witness giving evidence. It hasn't been put to any other witness who has given evidence to that effect that they are incorrect. My learned colleague now asks him what he relies on in order to conclude that the civilian population was deprived of electricity, fuel, water and transport. A number of witnesses have given evidence of -- in fact, countless witnesses have given evidence that the civilian population was deprived of electricity, fuel and water and transport from time to time. It hasn't been put to any of them that that was incorrect. My objection is that these questions seem to lack any probative value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Ierace, to clarify your objection because I did understand the question in the context of that the Bosnian Serb forces used that advantage to deprive its civilians of food, water, electricity and gas. I do agree with you that there has been, at numerous occasions, testimony that there might for longer or shorter periods of time have been no water, no electricity. But I understand the question as to the conclusion as a whole in its context. Am I right in understanding so then --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then, perhaps, Mr. Donia, the question -- the objection is denied, Mr. Ierace. The question is not specifically on whether there was shortage of water, electricity, gas or transportation, but what are the sources, as far as I understand, for your conclusion that this was a result of the advantage the Bosnian Serb forces had?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I am going to put this question to you again: Did you base this conclusion on your own personal investigation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: If you are asking if I did the research and prepared the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that you, yourself, gathered the documentation. Can you tell us specifically what documents you used this reference material in order to stress that the civilian population was being deprived of food?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: On page 14 of the English version of the report, I cited extensively the report of Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the special rapporteur of the UN Commission on Human Rights who wrote, "The seige, including the shelling of population centres and cutting off of supplies of food and other essential goods is another tactic. The city is shelled on a regular basis in what appears to be a deliberate attempt to spread terror among the population. Snipers shoot innocent victims. The mission visited the hospital and was able to see many civilian victims."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia, for reading this out for us. I am familiar with the report myself. I have quite simply reached the conclusion right now that your own personal research in relation to the conclusion is based on the document drawn up by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, the quote that you've just read out to us. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: This is one of the sources that I have cited in the report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if this is one of your sources, what other sources were available to you and what sources did you use in reaching your conclusion that the population was deprived of food?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think the sources are all apparent in the footnotes to the report. I cited the combination of deprivation of food, water, transportation and other essential goods, indicated that General Mladic made a statement on the 12th of May that it was his inattention to deprive the city of such things. It is consistently and repeatedly referred to in the report of the commission of experts and reported by journalists who visited the city at various times during the siege. I personally met many people in Sarajevo in 1994 who had lost 15 to 30 pounds in the course of the months after April 1992, and certainly saw numerous occasions that there were limitations on certain types of food that would be available, particularly fresh foods. But I think the sources that you are asking about are, in fact, multiple. They come from people who were there at the time and affirm that these basic commodities were provided only periodically and sometimes not at all in those months of the siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are telling us that your knowledge about the deprivation of the civilian population of food, you acquired during your stay in Sarajevo and your conversations with people who lived in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No, that is not the statement that I made. The statement that I made was that the sources for the deprivation of food, water, transportation, heat, are multiple. They come from journalists who are visiting the area. They come from United Nations observers who published their conclusions on a daily basis in the report of the commission of experts. They come from the stated intention of General Mladic to engage in such a strategy. I view my own personal statement or observations as but a very limited part of the source body which is extraordinarily wealthy in terms of attesting to that fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Donia. I already said that tomorrow we would be coming back to the minutes of the 12th of May, 1992 and the Defence would have some questions about those minutes. Now, while we are talking about the civilian population which was deprived of food, power, and water and so on and so forth, you told us that you visited Sarajevo on a number of occasions. Do you know how many times that you were in those war years in Sarajevo, 1992, 1993, 1994, how often or how many days was Sarajevo left without water supply? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Not for the -- no, I don't know the specific number. It was certainly without water supply for at least half of the days that I was there, in maybe 12, 14, days in 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge or did you try to find out that as a result of the water shortage -- that the water shortage in Sarajevo was a result of the power shortage in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that due to combat operations in the Sarajevo area during the fighting between the two armies, some transformer stations were damaged and that was the reason why there were power and water cuts in Sarajevo? Would that be acceptable to you, since we know that there were two armies and that in the city of Sarajevo and around it, there was fighting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, according to you, which were the sources that you rely on to conclude that there was no water, electricity or gas in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: I think I have given you that answer about five times, ma'am. I can recite again the sources, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. No, thank you. If these are the sources that you gave us when I asked you about the food shortage, thank you very much, there is no need to. So you still stand by those sources and you say that these sources hold true also when it comes to water and electricity?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- I object to the question for the same reasons I gave on the previous occasion. I think the wording of this question now incontrovertibly falls within the objection I made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the earlier objection then?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Simply, Mr. President, that it isn't in dispute, as I understand it, that there were those shortages and, therefore, there is no probative value in probing this witness as to what his sources were. Perhaps my friend could indicate if I am correct. Perhaps you can indicate if it is in dispute that there were shortages of water, electricity and gas during that period to the citizens of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my questions I directed at this part of Mr. Donia's conclusion because Mr. Donia has told us that the result -- that the result of the water, power and food shortage in the city was because of the shelling of the city. That is how the counsel put the question. I merely was trying to find out from Mr. Donia which other sources did he use to reach this conclusion. And we heard Mr. Donia's conclusion that it was Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki's report, of the special rapporteur. And in particular in my questions I touched upon the indictment period. From Mr. Donia's report, we see that Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki was in Sarajevo in the 24th of August, 1992. Mr. Donia told us that he was in Sarajevo in 1994, as well. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, let's just try to cut things short. Could you indicate where exactly Mr. Donia told that the result of the water, power and food -- water, power and food shortage was because of the shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the conclusion as I interpret it, says that they used that advantage to shell the city periodically, to damage and destroy its cultural and religious monuments and to deprive its civilian population of food, water, electricity, gas and transportation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was not the testimony of Mr. Donia. And would you then please first ask him whether the deprivation of civilian population of food, water, electricity, gas and transportation was a result of the shelling. Because that is an interpretation which is not...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first ask -- you are mixing up a lot of things and I would like you to be clearer. If Mr. Donia says that you asked a similar session for the fifth time - why, it may have been the fourth time - what was about water, gas, electricity, that was mixed up several times, so, please, would you be a bit more precise in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could be more precise but since Mr. Donia was in Sarajevo and he studied the history of the city, I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean more precise in questioning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you have any knowledge if the army of BH was responsible for power and water cuts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of what are you saying, no, are you answering no? Is it that you do not know or is it that it is not true that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was responsible for power and water cuts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: In response to your question, I have no knowledge if the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was responsible for power and water cuts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the end of your conclusion, you say that international observers increasingly feared a humanitarian catastrophe if the siege continued in place through the cold Bosnian winter. Can you tell us precisely which winter are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: My reference is to September 1992 here and so my statement here pertains to the coming winter of 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the siege of Sarajevo last, according to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Well, the siege of Sarajevo lasted until January of 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talk about the humanitarian catastrophe in your conclusion. Did you, being a historian, come by information, and if you did, which is that and what is that information? How many people starved to death or died of cold in Sarajevo during that period of time; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA
utterances.text: Your characterization of my statement isn't quite right. I stated that international observers increasingly feared humanitarian catastrophe if the siege continued through the cold Bosnian winter. I don't know a number for those who starved or died from starvation during the siege. My impression is that it is very difficult to separate out the multiple causes of some deaths during the siege because the factors were multiple. There was lack of food and water, lack of adequate medical supplies and then, in some cases, psychological factors that proved to be deadly. So I think it is hard to reach a number for that -- to answer that question precisely in any case, and I wouldn't know what that number is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe this would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we could adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a good suggestion. I will follow it, Ms. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pilipovic. We will adjourn until tomorrow, same courtroom, a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
